passages.title: How Bees Find a Flower
passages.text:
The biology club at Westbrook School planned to determine why bees visited one patch of flowering herbs more often than another. A preliminary count showed a striking difference despite the patches' similar colors and their proximity. Several students immediately concluded that bees preferred the stronger scent emitted by one variety. Their teacher suggested a narrower claim: the observed visits were consistent with a scent preference, but the students had not yet separated scent from nectar availability, flower shape, or exposure to afternoon shade.

To investigate, the club marked individual blossoms and arranged ten-minute observation intervals. Each group counted visits from the same marked position, recording temperature and cloud cover. During the morning, bees approached the strongly scented blossoms more often. The pattern weakened after noon, when the sun moved behind a nearby greenhouse and part of the garden entered shade. One student interpreted the change as proof that scent mattered only in the morning. Another noted that the shaded area was also cooler, so the change could reflect temperature or light rather than an altered preference.

The club then tried covering some flowers with mesh sleeves for a short period and uncovering them before counting visits. The method was intended to equalize recent insect traffic, but the sleeves also changed how much heat and moisture surrounded each blossom. The students could not simply treat the covered flowers as identical to uncovered ones. Worse, the varieties were planted in separate patches, so any difference between varieties was also a difference in location.

Their teacher proposed a more informative trial: arrange potted plants of both varieties in mixed, randomized positions, record whether visitors collected nectar or pollen, and repeat measurements at several times of day. The students also discussed the limitations of treating every arrival as a unique bee. Without marking individual insects, one persistent forager could contribute many recorded visits. Counting visits could still be useful, but it would not establish how many different bees chose each variety.

The club presented its original observations at a school exhibition, carefully distinguishing what it had recorded from what it hoped to test next. More visits had occurred near a particular variety under the conditions observed; the relative influence of scent remained uncertain. The exhibition's most important finding was methodological: an appealing biological explanation becomes persuasive only when the experiment can distinguish it from credible alternatives.

questions.prompt: Why does the teacher resist the club's initial explanation about scent?
choices: The flowers' similar colors prove that scent cannot matter.
The data show a difference in visits but do not isolate scent from other characteristics or conditions.
Bee preference is impossible to investigate through observation.
The first counts show that nectar availability was identical across patches.
questions.explanation: The initial visit difference could arise from scent, nectar, shape, or shade. Identifying a possible cause is different from testing whether it explains the effect.

questions.prompt: What makes the decline in the afternoon visit difference difficult to interpret?
choices: Shade and cooler conditions changed together, so either might explain the altered visit pattern.
The students had recorded no observations in the morning.
Both flower varieties were moved into an enclosed laboratory.
The bees were all marked and released elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Light and temperature vary together near the greenhouse. Without separating them, the students cannot attribute the changing pattern to one variable.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of planting each flower variety in a separate patch?
choices: It creates too many independent variables to count.
It guarantees that bees will select the more fragrant flowers.
Variety differences are entangled with location differences.
It prevents researchers from recording visits at intervals.
questions.explanation: A site effect—such as shade, soil, or wind—could appear to be a variety effect because each variety occupies a different location.

questions.prompt: Why are the mesh sleeves an imperfect attempt to standardize flowers before observation?
choices: Sleeves prevent insects from visiting every flower permanently.
Sleeves remove the need for controlling environmental conditions.
Sleeves make every flower smell identical.
Sleeves may themselves change blossom temperature and humidity.
questions.explanation: The sleeves alter the microenvironment, creating a potential treatment effect instead of solely equalizing recent insect exposure.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the unmarked-bee limitation?
choices: A high visit count may include repeated visits by fewer individual bees.
No visit recorded by the students actually occurred.
The number of unique bees always exceeds the number of visits.
A single bee can never visit the same flower twice.
questions.explanation: Without individual markings, visits cannot be equated with unique visitors; one bee may be recorded repeatedly.

questions.prompt: Which modification would most directly reduce location-based confounding?
choices: Extend each count from ten minutes to fifteen minutes while leaving the patches unchanged.
Mix potted plants of both varieties in randomized positions across the same area.
Record only the first insect seen each morning.
Ask observers which flower they personally find more fragrant.
questions.explanation: Randomized mixed positions separate variety identity from any single position's conditions. Longer counts or opinions do not fix the confound.

questions.prompt: Why does the proposed trial distinguish nectar-collecting from pollen-collecting visits?
choices: The two activities must involve different insect species.
Only nectar collection is affected by flower shape.
Visits motivated by different resources may not be explained by scent in the same way.
Pollen visits cannot be observed outdoors.
questions.explanation: Recording foraging activity lets investigators test whether a pattern is linked to distinct resources rather than treating every arrival as behaviorally equivalent.

questions.prompt: Which statement would overstate the evidence reported at the exhibition?
choices: The students observed unequal visit frequencies under certain conditions.
The students found reasons to control shade and temperature in later trials.
The students discussed randomized positions as a future improvement.
The students proved that stronger scent alone caused the morning preference.
questions.explanation: The observations did not isolate scent; several competing explanations remain plausible. The other statements describe recorded facts or design proposals.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the paragraph discussing sleeves and separate planting locations?
choices: It introduces methodological flaws that motivate a redesigned experiment.
It establishes that the original hypothesis must be false.
It shows that observers failed to count any bee visits.
It provides the final numerical result of the study.
questions.explanation: The paragraph identifies ways apparently controlled comparisons could remain biased and leads naturally to the randomized mixed-plant trial.

questions.prompt: Which general lesson does the passage most strongly support?
choices: An attractive hypothesis becomes reliable when observers agree about it.
Good experiments must distinguish a favored explanation from plausible competing causes.
Counting behavior is never a useful scientific method.
Repeated observations are unnecessary once a preliminary pattern emerges.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly emphasizes testing causal explanations against alternatives, not merely accumulating confirming observations.

passages.title: A Bridge Built Twice
passages.text:
The first bridge across the Alden River survived for only nineteen years. In town histories, its disappearance was often attributed to a single winter storm so violent that residents supposedly heard beams snapping from their bedrooms. The engineering museum preparing an exhibition initially expected to display this dramatic story alongside a drawing of the replacement bridge. Yet its curator found an awkward fact: a newspaper published the morning after the famous storm described damage to the riverbank but made no mention of a collapsed crossing.

The museum's research team turned to municipal accounts. Over the eight years before replacement, records showed repeated purchases of timber, repairs to the upstream supports, and payments to remove debris. Some entries were terse, describing only 'river works,' but the dates corresponded to unusually high water levels recorded at a nearby mill. This evidence suggested deterioration over many seasons rather than sudden destruction. It did not identify the exact moment the bridge became unsafe, and financial records could omit work performed without municipal payment.

A structural engineer explained that the bridge's original design had given it little clearance above seasonal floods. A strong current could push fallen branches against the supports, increasing pressure even during storms that did not break the crossing outright. The engineer considered the accumulated repairs consistent with this mechanism. But consistency was not confirmation: no surviving inspection report documented the supports' condition immediately before demolition. The town might also have replaced the bridge because greater commercial traffic demanded a wider roadway.

The researchers compared two later photographs, one showing a noticeably reinforced support and the other a larger replacement span. They carefully resisted reading the first image as proof that the bridge was near collapse. A reinforcement could be routine maintenance; a wider replacement could reflect changing needs as much as failure of the older structure. The museum consequently planned an exhibit with two parallel accounts: the memorable storm story and the slower pattern revealed by municipal spending and engineering constraints.

On opening day, a visitor complained that the exhibition deprived the town of its legend. The curator replied that the story remained part of local history—as evidence of what generations had believed and repeated—even if it could not stand alone as an explanation of the bridge's fate. The team's conclusion was intentionally narrower than its evidence collection: long-term vulnerability was plausible, a single catastrophic collapse was unverified, and the replacement decision may have combined safety with growing demand.

questions.prompt: Why does the newspaper report complicate the popular storm narrative?
choices: It describes immediate bank damage without reporting the claimed bridge collapse.
It establishes that no storm occurred that winter.
It proves the bridge was never repaired.
It names the person who designed the replacement.
questions.explanation: The report's silence on collapse weakens, though does not conclusively refute, the dramatic account. It does not negate the storm or later repairs.

questions.prompt: What is the most responsible interpretation of the repeated municipal repair payments?
choices: They prove the bridge collapsed every winter.
They suggest recurrent problems, although records may be incomplete or nonspecific.
They demonstrate that every repair was fraudulent.
They show that the town never considered replacement.
questions.explanation: The payments indicate recurring maintenance across years, while 'river works' entries and unpaid work limit a fully precise reconstruction.

questions.prompt: Why does the engineer discuss debris collecting against the supports?
choices: To show that timber bridges always fail without warning.
To demonstrate that photographs are unreliable.
To offer a plausible causal mechanism connecting high water to cumulative structural stress.
To establish the bridge was replaced solely because of heavier commercial traffic.
questions.explanation: Debris loading provides a mechanism consistent with repair records, not conclusive proof of collapse or a unique reason for replacement.

questions.prompt: Which discovery would most directly strengthen the claim that the original bridge was structurally unsafe near the time of replacement?
choices: A late-nineteenth-century poem celebrating the river.
A list of travelers who crossed the river decades earlier.
A photograph of the town square taken after demolition.
A dated engineering inspection identifying serious defects in the supports.
questions.explanation: An inspection close to replacement would directly document structural condition, whereas distant anecdotes and unrelated images would not.

questions.prompt: Why does the curator avoid treating the photograph of a reinforced support as proof of imminent failure?
choices: Reinforcement might reflect precautionary or routine maintenance rather than emergency deterioration.
Photographs cannot reveal any engineering details.
The image dates from after the bridge was demolished.
Any reinforced bridge must be newly built.
questions.explanation: The same visual evidence permits multiple reasonable interpretations. The photograph supports the fact of reinforcement, not the urgency that motivated it.

questions.prompt: How could growing commercial traffic alter the interpretation of the bridge's replacement?
choices: It would establish that the river had stopped flooding.
It could make expansion desirable even if the older bridge had not suffered a sudden collapse.
It would prove that the replacement was built from the original timber.
It would make earlier maintenance entries irrelevant.
questions.explanation: A wider bridge may respond to increased demand, so replacement cannot automatically be equated with catastrophic failure.

questions.prompt: What role does the local legend retain in the exhibit?
choices: It supplies a verified cause of the demolition.
It establishes that contemporary reports were deliberately censored.
It documents a tradition of remembering the event even where its factual explanation is uncertain.
It removes the need for any engineering evidence.
questions.explanation: The curator distinguishes what people believed from what occurred; the story remains evidence of collective memory, not conclusive engineering history.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion most closely matches the research team's findings?
choices: A single famous storm certainly destroyed the bridge.
Commercial development alone explains the replacement.
Municipal repair records can never establish useful historical patterns.
Recurring vulnerabilities are plausible, but the bridge's final condition and replacement motives are not conclusively established.
questions.explanation: Records and design suggest long-term risk while gaps and alternative motives prevent stronger claims.

questions.prompt: What is the primary effect of contrasting the storm legend with financial and structural evidence?
choices: It moves from a dramatic single-cause story to a more conditional, multi-cause interpretation.
It argues that legends have no historical significance.
It replaces a narrative with a set of unrelated anecdotes.
It demonstrates that every written record is inherently accurate.
questions.explanation: The contrast highlights how accumulated independent evidence can complicate a memorable simplified explanation.

questions.prompt: Which practice best characterizes the museum team's approach?
choices: Accept the oldest account because it is closest to the event.
Triangulate different sources, identify their limits, and separate plausible explanations from demonstrated facts.
Reject photographs as incapable of supporting any inference.
Choose a conclusion before examining records and preserve it despite contradictions.
questions.explanation: The team compares newspapers, payments, photographs and engineering reasoning while acknowledging what no source can establish alone.

passages.title: A Seat at the Table
passages.text:
Jonah entered the student policy club halfway through the semester. At his first meeting, members moved easily between names of committees, deadlines, and documents that meant nothing to him. The president asked whether anyone objected to the schedule for a neighborhood recycling campaign; silence followed, and the group approved it. Jonah had noticed that the proposed printing deadline came before the school board's decision on the campaign design, but he was reluctant to interrupt a discussion he barely understood.

After the meeting, the club secretary sent Jonah a folder of earlier minutes. He spent an evening reconstructing the sequence of approvals and learned that the board occasionally requested revisions. If that happened now, the club would have paid to print hundreds of flyers that it could no longer use. When Jonah asked the secretary whether the printing date was fixed, she replied that the printer offered a discount only until Friday. The conflict was therefore not simply a clerical mistake; delaying might cost money, while printing early risked waste.

At the next meeting, Jonah avoided announcing that the schedule was wrong. Instead, he asked what the club would do if the board requested changes after printing. The treasurer calculated that replacing the flyers would cost more than losing the discount. Another member noted that the board had approved similar campaigns without changes, but could not say how often. The club agreed to request a written design review before placing the order, even if the discount expired. The president thanked Jonah and explained that a new perspective had exposed an assumption the longtime members had stopped questioning.

The incident did not make Jonah an immediate leader. During subsequent meetings, he still struggled to follow procedural shorthand and sometimes needed someone to explain the history behind a vote. Nor did the club abandon its established habits because of one useful question. Instead, members began adding brief rationale notes to the minutes so that new volunteers could understand why decisions had been made. The modification helped experienced members as well: when two proposed events competed for the same equipment, old notes clarified which commitments were firm and which had only been tentative.

Jonah later reflected that he had mistaken fluency for competence. The veteran members spoke quickly because they shared context; their speed did not guarantee that every assumption was sound. His own hesitation had protected him from making an uninformed declaration, but it had nearly kept him from posing an important question. The experience suggested a more useful distinction: informed participation does not require pretending to know everything, but it does require enough preparation to identify the uncertainty worth bringing into a room.

questions.prompt: Why does Jonah remain silent at the first meeting despite spotting a possible scheduling problem?
choices: He has confirmed the printer will extend the discount.
He is reluctant to challenge a group whose procedures he does not yet understand.
He believes all campaign schedules are irrelevant.
He already knows the school board will approve the design.
questions.explanation: Jonah observes a mismatch but lacks the contextual confidence to interrupt. His reluctance does not mean he knows the risk is unimportant.

questions.prompt: What tension complicates the decision to postpone flyer printing?
choices: Waiting may lose a discount, but printing early may create expensive waste if revisions are required.
The secretary refuses to send minutes to new members.
The school board has permanently rejected the campaign.
The club is prohibited from using external printers.
questions.explanation: A lower current price competes with the potential cost of reprinting. The group's choice requires comparing contingent costs.

questions.prompt: Why does the statement that the board approved earlier campaigns without changes fail to settle the matter?
choices: Earlier approvals are unrelated to the board's authority.
Only written minutes can be evidence in school clubs.
Without a reliable frequency or guarantee, prior approvals do not rule out revisions now.
The printer's discount proves the board must approve the design.
questions.explanation: A history of approvals may inform probability but cannot guarantee an outcome, especially when the member cannot quantify the record.

questions.prompt: Why is Jonah's second-meeting question more productive than declaring the schedule wrong?
choices: It makes the president solely responsible for costs.
It avoids mentioning any actual scheduling issue.
It demonstrates that Jonah has superior authority over the board.
It invites the group to examine the consequence of an uncertain assumption.
questions.explanation: By asking about a plausible revision, Jonah prompts the treasurer's cost comparison and broader reasoning without claiming certainty.

questions.prompt: What does the president's reaction imply about group familiarity?
choices: Established routines can conceal assumptions from those who share them.
Experienced members are generally less intelligent than newcomers.
Every new member will identify the same scheduling risk.
The president had intentionally hidden the printing schedule.
questions.explanation: The remark suggests shared habits can go unexamined. It does not deny the experienced members' expertise or impute deception.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of adding rationale notes to meeting minutes?
choices: To replace all deliberation with fixed written instructions.
To preserve the reasoning behind decisions for later readers and reconsideration.
To prevent new volunteers from proposing revisions.
To make all tentative commitments legally binding.
questions.explanation: Documenting reasons helps both newcomers and veterans distinguish assumptions, commitments and choices.

questions.prompt: If the printing discount had lasted another month, what would change most directly in the club's decision?
choices: The risk of board revisions would disappear.
Flyers could no longer be printed.
The immediate financial cost of postponing the order would be reduced.
The president would lose the authority to set deadlines.
questions.explanation: Extending the discount removes one cost of waiting while leaving approval uncertainty intact.

questions.prompt: Which belief does Jonah most explicitly revise?
choices: Preparation is useful only for senior officers.
Every hesitation indicates intellectual weakness.
Fast meetings always produce poor decisions.
Speaking fluently within a group is not the same as reasoning well about its assumptions.
questions.explanation: Jonah sees that speed reflects shared context but does not guarantee sound judgment; his preparation enables a valuable question.

questions.prompt: Why does the author describe later meetings after Jonah's useful intervention?
choices: To show that a single success did not erase his adjustment difficulties or transform the whole club instantly.
To reveal that the printing order was eventually canceled.
To prove that the club stopped using meeting minutes.
To imply that the first discussion was imagined.
questions.explanation: The later details qualify a simplistic triumph narrative and show gradual mutual adaptation.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best captures the passage's understanding of participation?
choices: Effective membership requires unanimous agreement.
Useful participation combines preparation, intellectual humility, and willingness to question assumptions.
A newcomer should never speak without complete historical knowledge.
An outsider's perspective automatically outweighs an experienced member's judgment.
questions.explanation: Jonah gains enough context to ask a bounded, consequential question while admitting uncertainty. The passage neither glorifies ignorance nor demands total mastery.

passages.title: Darwin — Changing Habits and Adaptation
passages.text:
I will now give two or three instances of diversified and of changed habits in the individuals of the same species. When either case occurs, it would be easy for natural selection to fit the animal, by some modification of its structure, for its changed habits, or exclusively for one of its several different habits. But it is difficult to tell, and immaterial for us, whether habits generally change first and structure afterwards; or whether slight modifications of structure lead to changed habits; both probably often change almost simultaneously. Of cases of changed habits it will suffice merely to allude to that of the many British insects which now feed on exotic plants, or exclusively on artificial substances. Of diversified habits innumerable instances could be given: I have often watched a tyrant flycatcher (Saurophagus sulphuratus) in South America, hovering over one spot and then proceeding to another, like a kestrel, and at other times standing stationary on the margin of water, and then dashing like a kingfisher at a fish. In our own country the larger titmouse (Parus major) may be seen climbing branches, almost like a creeper; it often, like a shrike, kills small birds by blows on the head; and I have many times seen and heard it hammering the seeds of the yew on a branch, and thus breaking them like a nuthatch. In North America the black bear was seen by Hearne swimming for hours with widely open mouth, thus catching, like a whale, insects in the water. Even in so extreme a case as this, if the supply of insects were constant, and if better adapted competitors did not already exist in the country, I can see no difficulty in a race of bears being rendered, by natural selection, more and more aquatic in their structure and habits, with larger and larger mouths, till a creature was produced as monstrous as a whale.

As we sometimes see individuals of a species following habits widely different from those both of their own species and of the other species of the same genus, we might expect, on my theory, that such individuals would occasionally have given rise to new species, having anomalous habits, and with their structure either slightly or considerably modified from that of their proper type. And such instances do occur in nature. Can a more striking instance of adaptation be given than that of a woodpecker for climbing trees and for seizing insects in the chinks of the bark? Yet in North America there are woodpeckers which feed largely on fruit, and others with elongated wings which chase insects on the wing; and on the plains of La Plata, where not a tree grows, there is a woodpecker, which in every essential part of its organisation, even in its colouring, in the harsh tone of its voice, and undulatory flight, told me plainly of its close blood-relationship to our common species; yet it is a woodpecker which never climbs a tree!

questions.prompt: What uncertainty does Darwin acknowledge about the relationship between habits and bodily structure?
choices: He cannot always determine whether changed behavior precedes structural change or vice versa.
He knows habits can never vary.
He argues all structural change happens in a single generation.
He claims adaptations never affect behavior.
questions.explanation: He explicitly says the order is difficult to tell and that both may change nearly simultaneously.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: How do the examples of the flycatcher and titmouse function?
choices: They prove every bird species eats identical prey.
They provide anecdotes about individual owners.
They illustrate that members of a species can employ different feeding behaviors.
They show these birds have already become different species.
questions.explanation: The behaviors illustrate variety in habits within species rather than documented speciation.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: What conditions are attached to Darwin's speculative bear-to-aquatic-form example?
choices: The bears must already be whales.
A sustained insect food supply and absence of better-adapted competitors might favor increasingly aquatic traits.
The bears must stop reproducing.
All animals must live in identical habitats.
questions.explanation: Darwin explicitly qualifies the hypothetical by resource constancy and competitive conditions.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: Which statement would overstate Darwin's account of the black bear?
choices: A bear was reported feeding while swimming.
Darwin treats it as an illustration of behavioral flexibility.
He imagines long-term selection under particular circumstances.
He documents the observed evolution of that bear population into whales.
questions.explanation: The observed behavior and speculative long-term possibility are distinct; he does not document a bear lineage evolving into whales.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: How does the discussion connect behavioral diversity to natural selection?
choices: A habit may expose different uses of an environment, allowing selection to favor structures better suited to it.
Natural selection makes all organisms behave identically.
Every learned act permanently changes inherited traits immediately.
Species must first abandon all existing foods.
questions.explanation: Darwin proposes that altered or varied habits provide contexts in which structural modifications can be selected.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: Why is the woodpecker living where no trees grow important to the argument?
choices: It establishes woodpeckers are not birds.
It disproves the existence of common ancestry.
It challenges a rigid assumption that species traits require identical habitats and behaviors everywhere.
It demonstrates that all woodpeckers are incapable of climbing.
questions.explanation: The tree-less habitat example illustrates divergence in lifestyle despite anatomical and behavioral evidence of relatedness.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: What role does 'might expect, on my theory' play?
choices: It makes the prediction a demonstrated certainty.
It presents a hypothesis-derived expectation rather than disguising it as a universally observed fact.
It indicates the author has abandoned his theory.
It shows he is describing only a fictional narrative.
questions.explanation: The wording marks a prediction consistent with his theoretical framework, inviting comparison with cases.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: What does Darwin's comparison of the plains woodpecker with familiar species emphasize?
choices: Their different calls prove no relationship.
Only plumage color matters for classification.
Bird behavior has no connection to anatomy.
Shared organization and vocal or flight traits can suggest relatedness despite different habits.
questions.explanation: He cites anatomical, coloring, voice and flight similarities in arguing blood-relationship despite the bird's unusual habitat.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: Which inference is not warranted by the passage alone?
choices: Every observed case proves the precise historical sequence of genetic changes that produced it.
Habit diversity can be observed within species.
Behavioral differences may offer starting points for further hypotheses.
The author uses specific examples to motivate a general possibility.
questions.explanation: The passage offers observations and theoretical reasoning, not complete genetic histories of the cases.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

questions.prompt: Which thesis most closely links the varied examples?
choices: Species are incapable of changing habits.
Structural similarity always requires identical behavior.
Variation in behavior can coexist with shared ancestry and may interact with long-term structural adaptation.
Habits are entirely independent of environmental conditions.
questions.explanation: The author repeatedly links diversified habits, selection and the possibility of structural change while retaining common organization.
questions.evidenceQuoteOrLocation: On the Origin of Species — variation of habits and adaptation

passages.title: A Cleaner Harbor
passages.text:
Every autumn storm pushed bottles, food wrappers, and fragments of packaging from a drainage canal into Ashport Harbor. Volunteers had spent years collecting litter from the docks, but their work began only after plastic had dispersed among moored boats and tidal marshes. Municipal engineers proposed installing a floating barrier near the canal outlet to intercept debris earlier. Local merchants welcomed the plan, while boat operators worried that a barrier might block navigation or divert floating waste toward private docks.

The engineers constructed a curved boom with an opening for small boats. They counted and weighed material captured after several rainfall events. The barrier collected hundreds of objects, which appeared to demonstrate success. Yet the collected weight depended on storm size: a powerful storm could carry more waste into the canal even if the barrier captured a smaller fraction of the total. To estimate effectiveness, the team needed a denominator—the amount of litter entering the canal—not just the amount recovered at the boom.

A second difficulty emerged when the team inspected the contents of the collected debris. Many objects were soaked, so their weight included water. Some heavy items were branches that would have entered the harbor regardless of the city's plastic-litter campaign. Volunteers began separating categories and recording both dry mass and item counts. The two measures sometimes told different stories: a few waterlogged objects dominated the mass while numerous fragments accounted for most of the pieces. Neither measure was inherently wrong, but each represented a different aspect of the problem.

During the next storm, fast water pressed against the boom and briefly pushed debris beneath it. An engineer proposed tightening the barrier; a harbor pilot warned that a tighter opening might create hazardous currents for small craft. The city chose to reinforce the anchoring points and observe how the revised system performed across a range of water levels. It also installed a temporary downstream net to sample escaping objects, although the net could not capture everything and required its own maintenance.

The final report avoided calling the barrier a complete solution. It had visibly reduced some litter reaching the docks under tested conditions, but long-term performance, safety, maintenance cost, and upstream disposal habits still mattered. The authors recommended pairing interception with efforts to prevent litter entering drains in the first place. A cleaner harbor, they argued, would depend not merely on how much waste could be caught at one point but on whether the city reduced the flow of waste through the entire system.

questions.prompt: Why does the report argue that the weight of collected debris alone cannot establish barrier efficiency?
choices: Weights are always less accurate than counting objects.
The collection amount must be compared with the total litter entering the canal, which varies with storms.
The barrier is legally required to capture all objects.
Material recovered after a storm has no relation to litter in the water.
questions.explanation: Without a denominator, more recovered waste could reflect greater inflow rather than a higher interception rate.

questions.prompt: How do the conflicting dry-mass and object-count results illustrate a measurement problem?
choices: Counting objects automatically proves a higher ecological impact.
Dry mass can never be measured accurately.
Different metrics emphasize different features of the debris and can change the apparent magnitude of success.
Both metrics must yield the same ranking to be valid.
questions.explanation: Heavy objects dominate mass, while small fragments dominate counts. Each metric is useful for a different question.

questions.prompt: Why does the harbor pilot oppose immediately tightening the opening?
choices: The proposed change could improve capture while making navigation currents more dangerous.
The original boom has already blocked every vessel.
Small boats never enter the canal.
The collected debris includes waterlogged items.
questions.explanation: The pilot points to a safety cost of maximizing collection, requiring engineers to balance effectiveness against navigability.

questions.prompt: What does the temporary downstream net contribute to the evaluation?
choices: It proves that all waste bypassing the barrier has been counted.
It removes the need for maintaining the barrier.
It measures upstream litter generation independently of storm size.
It offers an imperfect estimate of objects escaping interception.
questions.explanation: The net samples material that passes the boom but cannot catch everything. It adds a missing outcome estimate without proving total containment.

questions.prompt: Why do the authors distinguish branches from plastic packaging in the collection?
choices: Branches are always more dangerous to people than plastic.
A campaign targeting plastic pollution needs categories that distinguish plastic from other storm-borne material.
All tree debris is man-made pollution.
Branches and plastic behave identically in water.
questions.explanation: Including unrelated natural debris can exaggerate the plastic-specific impact of the intervention, even if branches still require management.

questions.prompt: Which claim exceeds the evidence available at the end of the trial?
choices: The barrier collected floating objects after multiple storms.
The anchoring points were reinforced following fast-water observations.
The barrier permanently eliminated all harbor litter without introducing other costs.
The report considered safety and maintenance.
questions.explanation: Limited observations do not establish complete, permanent elimination or absence of costs.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of introducing merchants and boat operators in the opening paragraph?
choices: To show that different stakeholders value different consequences of the same intervention.
To prove that commercial interests determine environmental outcomes.
To establish that the municipal engineers fabricated their observations.
To identify the source of every piece of plastic.
questions.explanation: The groups represent the competing priorities—cleaner docks and safe navigation—that later shape design decisions.

questions.prompt: Why does the conclusion call for upstream waste prevention?
choices: Because the boom demonstrably captures no plastic.
Because downstream cleanups are legally forbidden.
Because preventing litter makes storm measurements unnecessary.
Because capture at one point leaves the underlying inflow and other pathways of pollution unresolved.
questions.explanation: The barrier is only one intervention in the system; reducing entry into drains addresses the source rather than solely intercepting its consequences.

questions.prompt: Which result would best support the claim that the reinforced barrier improved performance without unacceptable safety costs?
choices: A photograph of the barrier at low tide.
Higher capture fractions across comparable storms, alongside documented safe boat passages.
An increased weight of wet branches after a larger storm.
More volunteers expressing approval at the harbor meeting.
questions.explanation: Capture fractions control for incoming debris, while safe passage records address the competing navigation concern.

questions.prompt: Which general principle most clearly informs the engineering team's recommendations?
choices: A single positive observation proves a technological intervention should be permanent.
Environmental changes should be judged only by the amount of material collected.
An intervention must be evaluated with relevant denominators, unintended effects, and system-wide alternatives.
Safety concerns should always override environmental goals without investigation.
questions.explanation: The report links comparative effectiveness, measurement choice, navigation risk, and upstream prevention.

passages.title: Frankenstein — Creation and Revulsion
passages.text:
The different accidents of life are not so changeable as the feelings of human nature. I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body. For this I had deprived myself of rest and health. I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart. Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created, I rushed out of the room and continued a long time traversing my bed-chamber, unable to compose my mind to sleep. At length lassitude succeeded to the tumult I had before endured, and I threw myself on the bed in my clothes, endeavouring to seek a few moments of forgetfulness. But it was in vain; I slept, indeed, but I was disturbed by the wildest dreams. I thought I saw Elizabeth, in the bloom of health, walking in the streets of Ingolstadt. Delighted and surprised, I embraced her, but as I imprinted the first kiss on her lips, they became livid with the hue of death; her features appeared to change, and I thought that I held the corpse of my dead mother in my arms; a shroud enveloped her form, and I saw the grave-worms crawling in the folds of the flannel. I started from my sleep with horror; a cold dew covered my forehead, my teeth chattered, and every limb became convulsed; when, by the dim and yellow light of the moon, as it forced its way through the window shutters, I beheld the wretch--the miserable monster whom I had created. He held up the curtain of the bed; and his eyes, if eyes they may be called, were fixed on me. His jaws opened, and he muttered some inarticulate sounds, while a grin wrinkled his cheeks. He might have spoken, but I did not hear; one hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me, but I escaped and rushed downstairs. I took refuge in the courtyard belonging to the house which I inhabited, where I remained during the rest of the night, walking up and down in the greatest agitation, listening attentively, catching and fearing each sound as if it were to announce the approach of the demoniacal corpse to which I had so miserably given life.

Oh! No mortal could support the horror of that countenance. A mummy again endued with animation could not be so hideous as that wretch. I had gazed on him while unfinished; he was ugly then, but when those muscles and joints were rendered capable of motion, it became a thing such as even Dante could not have conceived.

I passed the night wretchedly. Sometimes my pulse beat so quickly and hardly that I felt the palpitation of every artery; at others, I nearly sank to the ground through languor and extreme weakness. Mingled with this horror, I felt the bitterness of disappointment; dreams that had been my food and pleasant rest for so long a space were now become a hell to me; and the change was so rapid, the overthrow so complete!

passages.title: The Federalist Papers — Can a Large Republic Function?
passages.text:
As the natural limit of a democracy is that distance from the central point which will just permit the most remote citizens to assemble as often as their public functions demand, and will include no greater number than can join in those functions; so the natural limit of a republic is that distance from the centre which will barely allow the representatives to meet as often as may be necessary for the administration of public affairs. Can it be said that the limits of the United States exceed this distance? It will not be said by those who recollect that the Atlantic coast is the longest side of the Union, that during the term of thirteen years, the representatives of the States have been almost continually assembled, and that the members from the most distant States are not chargeable with greater intermissions of attendance than those from the States in the neighborhood of Congress.

That we may form a juster estimate with regard to this interesting subject, let us resort to the actual dimensions of the Union. The limits, as fixed by the treaty of peace, are: on the east the Atlantic, on the south the latitude of thirty-one degrees, on the west the Mississippi, and on the north an irregular line running in some instances beyond the forty-fifth degree, in others falling as low as the forty-second. The southern shore of Lake Erie lies below that latitude. Computing the distance between the thirty-first and forty-fifth degrees, it amounts to nine hundred and seventy-three common miles; computing it from thirty-one to forty-two degrees, to seven hundred and sixty-four miles and a half. Taking the mean for the distance, the amount will be eight hundred and sixty-eight miles and three-fourths. The mean distance from the Atlantic to the Mississippi does not probably exceed seven hundred and fifty miles. On a comparison of this extent with that of several countries in Europe, the practicability of rendering our system commensurate to it appears to be demonstrable. It is not a great deal larger than Germany, where a diet representing the whole empire is continually assembled; or than Poland before the late dismemberment, where another national diet was the depositary of the supreme power. Passing by France and Spain, we find that in Great Britain, inferior as it may be in size, the representatives of the northern extremity of the island have as far to travel to the national council as will be required of those of the most remote parts of the Union.

Favorable as this view of the subject may be, some observations remain which will place it in a light still more satisfactory.

In the first place it is to be remembered that the general government is not to be charged with the whole power of making and administering laws. Its jurisdiction is limited to certain enumerated objects, which concern all the members of the republic, but which are not to be attained by the separate provisions of any. The subordinate governments, which can extend their care to all those other subjects which can be separately provided for, will retain their due authority and activity. Were it proposed by the plan of the convention to abolish the governments of the particular States, its adversaries would have some ground for their objection; though it would not be difficult to show that if they were abolished the general government would be compelled, by the principle of self-preservation, to reinstate them in their proper jurisdiction.

passages.title: Thoreau — The Cost of Living
passages.text:
So that all the pecuniary outgoes, excepting for washing and mending, which for the most part were done out of the house, and their bills have not yet been received--and these are all and more than all the ways by which money necessarily goes out in this part of the world--were

House................................. $ 28.12-1/2 Farm one year........................... 14.72-1/2 Food eight months....................... 8.74 Clothing, etc., eight months............ 8.40-3/4 Oil, etc., eight months................. 2.00 ------------ In all............................ $ 61.99-3/4

I address myself now to those of my readers who have a living to get. And to meet this I have for farm produce sold

$23.44 Earned by day-labor.................... 13.34 -------- In all............................. $36.78,

which subtracted from the sum of the outgoes leaves a balance of $25.21-3/4 on the one side--this being very nearly the means with which I started, and the measure of expenses to be incurred--and on the other, beside the leisure and independence and health thus secured, a comfortable house for me as long as I choose to occupy it.

These statistics, however accidental and therefore uninstructive they may appear, as they have a certain completeness, have a certain value also. Nothing was given me of which I have not rendered some account. It appears from the above estimate, that my food alone cost me in money about twenty-seven cents a week. It was, for nearly two years after this, rye and Indian meal without yeast, potatoes, rice, a very little salt pork, molasses, and salt; and my drink, water. It was fit that I should live on rice, mainly, who love so well the philosophy of India. To meet the objections of some inveterate cavillers, I may as well state, that if I dined out occasionally, as I always had done, and I trust shall have opportunities to do again, it was frequently to the detriment of my domestic arrangements. But the dining out, being, as I have stated, a constant element, does not in the least affect a comparative statement like this.

I learned from my two years' experience that it would cost incredibly little trouble to obtain one's necessary food, even in this latitude; that a man may use as simple a diet as the animals, and yet retain health and strength. I have made a satisfactory dinner, satisfactory on several accounts, simply off a dish of purslane (_Portulaca oleracea_) which I gathered in my cornfield, boiled and salted. I give the Latin on account of the savoriness of the trivial name. And pray what more can a reasonable man desire, in peaceful times, in ordinary noons, than a sufficient number of ears of green sweet corn boiled, with the addition of salt? Even the little variety which I used was a yielding to the demands of appetite, and not of health. Yet men have come to such a pass that they frequently starve, not for want of necessaries, but for want of luxuries; and I know a good woman who thinks that her son lost his life because he took to drinking water only.

passages.title: Darwin — Fertility and Changing Conditions
passages.text:
In regard to the sterility of hybrids, in which the sexual elements are imperfectly developed, the case is very different. I have more than once alluded to a large body of facts, which I have collected, showing that when animals and plants are removed from their natural conditions, they are extremely liable to have their reproductive systems seriously affected. This, in fact, is the great bar to the domestication of animals. Between the sterility thus superinduced and that of hybrids, there are many points of similarity. In both cases the sterility is independent of general health, and is often accompanied by excess of size or great luxuriance. In both cases, the sterility occurs in various degrees; in both, the male element is the most liable to be affected; but sometimes the female more than the male. In both, the tendency goes to a certain extent with systematic affinity, for whole groups of animals and plants are rendered impotent by the same unnatural conditions; and whole groups of species tend to produce sterile hybrids. On the other hand, one species in a group will sometimes resist great changes of conditions with unimpaired fertility; and certain species in a group will produce unusually fertile hybrids. No one can tell, till he tries, whether any particular animal will breed under confinement or any plant seed freely under culture; nor can he tell, till he tries, whether any two species of a genus will produce more or less sterile hybrids. Lastly, when organic beings are placed during several generations under conditions not natural to them, they are extremely liable to vary, which is due, as I believe, to their reproductive systems having been specially affected, though in a lesser degree than when sterility ensues. So it is with hybrids, for hybrids in successive generations are eminently liable to vary, as every experimentalist has observed.

Thus we see that when organic beings are placed under new and unnatural conditions, and when hybrids are produced by the unnatural crossing of two species, the reproductive system, independently of the general state of health, is affected by sterility in a very similar manner. In the one case, the conditions of life have been disturbed, though often in so slight a degree as to be inappreciable by us; in the other case, or that of hybrids, the external conditions have remained the same, but the organisation has been disturbed by two different structures and constitutions having been blended into one. For it is scarcely possible that two organisations should be compounded into one, without some disturbance occurring in the development, or periodical action, or mutual relation of the different parts and organs one to another, or to the conditions of life. When hybrids are able to breed inter se, they transmit to their offspring from generation to generation the same compounded organisation, and hence we need not be surprised that their sterility, though in some degree variable, rarely diminishes.

passages.title: Austen — Wickham's Account of Darcy
passages.text:
He shook his head. "I wish I could call her amiable. It gives me pain to speak ill of a Darcy. But she is too much like her brother--very, very proud. As a child, she was affectionate and pleasing, and extremely fond of me; and I have devoted hours and hours to her amusement. But she is nothing to me now. She is a handsome girl, about fifteen or sixteen, and, I understand, highly accomplished. Since her father's death, her home has been London, where a lady lives with her, and superintends her education."

After many pauses and many trials of other subjects, Elizabeth could not help reverting once more to the first, and saying:

"I am astonished at his intimacy with Mr. Bingley! How can Mr. Bingley, who seems good humour itself, and is, I really believe, truly amiable, be in friendship with such a man? How can they suit each other? Do you know Mr. Bingley?"

"Not at all."

"He is a sweet-tempered, amiable, charming man. He cannot know what Mr. Darcy is."

"Probably not; but Mr. Darcy can please where he chooses. He does not want abilities. He can be a conversible companion if he thinks it worth his while. Among those who are at all his equals in consequence, he is a very different man from what he is to the less prosperous. His pride never deserts him; but with the rich he is liberal-minded, just, sincere, rational, honourable, and perhaps agreeable--allowing something for fortune and figure."

The whist party soon afterwards breaking up, the players gathered round the other table and Mr. Collins took his station between his cousin Elizabeth and Mrs. Phillips. The usual inquiries as to his success were made by the latter. It had not been very great; he had lost every point; but when Mrs. Phillips began to express her concern thereupon, he assured her with much earnest gravity that it was not of the least importance, that he considered the money as a mere trifle, and begged that she would not make herself uneasy.

"I know very well, madam," said he, "that when persons sit down to a card-table, they must take their chances of these things, and happily I am not in such circumstances as to make five shillings any object. There are undoubtedly many who could not say the same, but thanks to Lady Catherine de Bourgh, I am removed far beyond the necessity of regarding little matters."

Mr. Wickham's attention was caught; and after observing Mr. Collins for a few moments, he asked Elizabeth in a low voice whether her relation was very intimately acquainted with the family of de Bourgh.

"Lady Catherine de Bourgh," she replied, "has very lately given him a living. I hardly know how Mr. Collins was first introduced to her notice, but he certainly has not known her long."

passages.title: Wells — The Time Traveller's Testimony
passages.text:
'I'd give a shilling a line for a verbatim note,' said the Editor. The Time Traveller pushed his glass towards the Silent Man and rang it with his fingernail; at which the Silent Man, who had been staring at his face, started convulsively, and poured him wine. The rest of the dinner was uncomfortable. For my own part, sudden questions kept on rising to my lips, and I dare say it was the same with the others. The Journalist tried to relieve the tension by telling anecdotes of Hettie Potter. The Time Traveller devoted his attention to his dinner, and displayed the appetite of a tramp. The Medical Man smoked a cigarette, and watched the Time Traveller through his eyelashes. The Silent Man seemed even more clumsy than usual, and drank champagne with regularity and determination out of sheer nervousness. At last the Time Traveller pushed his plate away, and looked round us. 'I suppose I must apologize,' he said. 'I was simply starving. I've had a most amazing time.' He reached out his hand for a cigar, and cut the end. 'But come into the smoking-room. It's too long a story to tell over greasy plates.' And ringing the bell in passing, he led the way into the adjoining room.

'You have told Blank, and Dash, and Chose about the machine?' he said to me, leaning back in his easy-chair and naming the three new guests.

'But the thing's a mere paradox,' said the Editor.

'I can't argue to-night. I don't mind telling you the story, but I can't argue. I will,' he went on, 'tell you the story of what has happened to me, if you like, but you must refrain from interruptions. I want to tell it. Badly. Most of it will sound like lying. So be it! It's true--every word of it, all the same. I was in my laboratory at four o'clock, and since then ... I've lived eight days ... such days as no human being ever lived before! I'm nearly worn out, but I shan't sleep till I've told this thing over to you. Then I shall go to bed. But no interruptions! Is it agreed?'

'Agreed,' said the Editor, and the rest of us echoed 'Agreed.' And with that the Time Traveller began his story as I have set it forth. He sat back in his chair at first, and spoke like a weary man. Afterwards he got more animated. In writing it down I feel with only too much keenness the inadequacy of pen and ink--and, above all, my own inadequacy--to express its quality. You read, I will suppose, attentively enough; but you cannot see the speaker's white, sincere face in the bright circle of the little lamp, nor hear the intonation of his voice. You cannot know how his expression followed the turns of his story! Most of us hearers were in shadow, for the candles in the smoking-room had not been lighted, and only the face of the Journalist and the legs of the Silent Man from the knees downward were illuminated. At first we glanced now and again at each other. After a time we ceased to do that, and looked only at the Time Traveller's face.

passages.title: Douglass — Literacy and the Institution of Slavery
passages.text:
My mistress was, as I have said, a kind and tender-hearted woman; and in the simplicity of her soul she commenced, when I first went to live with her, to treat me as she supposed one human being ought to treat another. In entering upon the duties of a slaveholder, she did not seem to perceive that I sustained to her the relation of a mere chattel, and that for her to treat me as a human being was not only wrong, but dangerously so. Slavery proved as injurious to her as it did to me. When I went there, she was a pious, warm, and tender-hearted woman. There was no sorrow or suffering for which she had not a tear. She had bread for the hungry, clothes for the naked, and comfort for every mourner that came within her reach. Slavery soon proved its ability to divest her of these heavenly qualities. Under its influence, the tender heart became stone, and the lamblike disposition gave way to one of tiger-like fierceness. The first step in her downward course was in her ceasing to instruct me. She now commenced to practise her husband's precepts. She finally became even more violent in her opposition than her husband himself. She was not satisfied with simply doing as well as he had commanded; she seemed anxious to do better. Nothing seemed to make her more angry than to see me with a newspaper. She seemed to think that here lay the danger. I have had her rush at me with a face made all up of fury, and snatch from me a newspaper, in a manner that fully revealed her apprehension. She was an apt woman; and a little experience soon demonstrated, to her satisfaction, that education and slavery were incompatible with each other.

From this time I was most narrowly watched. If I was in a separate room any considerable length of time, I was sure to be suspected of having a book, and was at once called to give an account of myself. All this, however, was too late. The first step had been taken. Mistress, in teaching me the alphabet, had given me the _inch,_ and no precaution could prevent me from taking the _ell._

The plan which I adopted, and the one by which I was most successful, was that of making friends of all the little white boys whom I met in the street. As many of these as I could, I converted into teachers. With their kindly aid, obtained at different times and in different places, I finally succeeded in learning to read. When I was sent of errands, I always took my book with me, and by going one part of my errand quickly, I found time to get a lesson before my return. I used also to carry bread with me, enough of which was always in the house, and to which I was always welcome; for I was much better off in this regard than many of the poor white children in our neighborhood. This bread I used to bestow upon the hungry little urchins, who, in return, would give me that more valuable bread of knowledge. I am strongly tempted to give the names of two or three of those little boys, as a testimonial of the gratitude and affection I bear them; but prudence forbids;--not that it would injure me, but it might embarrass them; for it is almost an unpardonable offence to teach slaves to read in this Christian country. It is enough to say of the dear little fellows, that they lived on Philpot Street, very near Durgin and Bailey's ship-yard. I used to talk this matter of slavery over with them. I would sometimes say to them, I wished I could be as free as they would be when they got to be men. "You will be free as soon as you are twenty-one, _but I am a slave for life!_ Have not I as good a right to be free as you have?" These words used to trouble them; they would express for me the liveliest sympathy, and console me with the hope that something would occur by which I might be free.

passages.title: Wollstonecraft — Education and Social Expectations
passages.text:
In the middle rank of life, to continue the comparison, men, in their youth, are prepared for professions, and marriage is not considered as the grand feature in their lives; whilst women, on the contrary, have no other scheme to sharpen their faculties. It is not business, extensive plans, or any of the excursive flights of ambition, that engross their attention; no, their thoughts are not employed in rearing such noble structures. To rise in the world, and have the liberty of running from pleasure to pleasure, they must marry advantageously, and to this object their time is sacrificed, and their persons often legally prostituted. A man, when he enters any profession, has his eye steadily fixed on some future advantage (and the mind gains great strength by having all its efforts directed to one point) and, full of his business, pleasure is considered as mere relaxation; whilst women seek for pleasure as the main purpose of existence. In fact, from the education which they receive from society, the love of pleasure may be said to govern them all; but does this prove that there is a sex in souls? It would be just as rational to declare, that the courtiers in France, when a destructive system of despotism had formed their character, were not men, because liberty, virtue, and humanity, were sacrificed to pleasure and vanity. Fatal passions, which have ever domineered over the WHOLE race!

The same love of pleasure, fostered by the whole tendency of their education, gives a trifling turn to the conduct of women in most circumstances: for instance, they are ever anxious about secondary things; and on the watch for adventures, instead of being occupied by duties.

A man, when he undertakes a journey, has, in general the end in view; a woman thinks more of the incidental occurrences, the strange things that may possibly occur on the road; the impression that she may make on her fellow travellers; and, above all, she is anxiously intent on the care of the finery that she carries with her, which is more than ever a part of herself, when going to figure on a new scene; when, to use an apt French turn of expression, she is going to produce a sensation. Can dignity of mind exist with such trivial cares?

In short, women, in general, as well as the rich of both sexes, have acquired all the follies and vices of civilization, and missed the useful fruit. It is not necessary for me always to premise, that I speak of the condition of the whole sex, leaving exceptions out of the question. Their senses are inflamed, and their understandings neglected; consequently they become the prey of their senses, delicately termed sensibility, and are blown about by every momentary gust of feeling. They are, therefore, in a much worse condition than they would be in, were they in a state nearer to nature. Ever restless and anxious, their over exercised sensibility not only renders them uncomfortable themselves, but troublesome, to use a soft phrase, to others. All their thoughts turn on things calculated to excite emotion; and, feeling, when they should reason, their conduct is unstable, and their opinions are wavering, not the wavering produced by deliberation or progressive views, but by contradictory emotions. By fits and starts they are warm in many pursuits; yet this warmth, never concentrated into perseverance, soon exhausts itself; exhaled by its own heat, or meeting with some other fleeting passion, to which reason has never given any specific gravity, neutrality ensues. Miserable, indeed, must be that being whose cultivation of mind has only tended to inflame its passions! A distinction should be made between inflaming and strengthening them. The passions thus pampered, whilst the judgment is left unformed, what can be expected to ensue? Undoubtedly, a mixture of madness and folly!

passages.title: Shelley — Victor's Silence and Guilt
passages.text:
No one can conceive the anguish I suffered during the remainder of the night, which I spent, cold and wet, in the open air. But I did not feel the inconvenience of the weather; my imagination was busy in scenes of evil and despair. I considered the being whom I had cast among mankind, and endowed with the will and power to effect purposes of horror, such as the deed which he had now done, nearly in the light of my own vampire, my own spirit let loose from the grave, and forced to destroy all that was dear to me.

Day dawned; and I directed my steps towards the town. The gates were open, and I hastened to my father's house. My first thought was to discover what I knew of the murderer, and cause instant pursuit to be made. But I paused when I reflected on the story that I had to tell. A being whom I myself had formed, and endued with life, had met me at midnight among the precipices of an inaccessible mountain. I remembered also the nervous fever with which I had been seized just at the time that I dated my creation, and which would give an air of delirium to a tale otherwise so utterly improbable. I well knew that if any other had communicated such a relation to me, I should have looked upon it as the ravings of insanity. Besides, the strange nature of the animal would elude all pursuit, even if I were so far credited as to persuade my relatives to commence it. And then of what use would be pursuit? Who could arrest a creature capable of scaling the overhanging sides of Mont Saleve? These reflections determined me, and I resolved to remain silent.

It was about five in the morning when I entered my father's house. I told the servants not to disturb the family, and went into the library to attend their usual hour of rising.

Six years had elapsed, passed in a dream but for one indelible trace, and I stood in the same place where I had last embraced my father before my departure for Ingolstadt. Beloved and venerable parent! He still remained to me. I gazed on the picture of my mother, which stood over the mantel-piece. It was an historical subject, painted at my father's desire, and represented Caroline Beaufort in an agony of despair, kneeling by the coffin of her dead father. Her garb was rustic, and her cheek pale; but there was an air of dignity and beauty, that hardly permitted the sentiment of pity. Below this picture was a miniature of William; and my tears flowed when I looked upon it. While I was thus engaged, Ernest entered: he had heard me arrive, and hastened to welcome me: "Welcome, my dearest Victor," said he. "Ah! I wish you had come three months ago, and then you would have found us all joyous and delighted. You come to us now to share a misery which nothing can alleviate; yet your presence will, I hope, revive our father, who seems sinking under his misfortune; and your persuasions will induce poor Elizabeth to cease her vain and tormenting self-accusations.--Poor William! he was our darling and our pride!"

passages.title: The Federalist Papers — Revenue and National Authority
passages.text:
In the Ottoman or Turkish empire, the sovereign, though in other respects absolute master of the lives and fortunes of his subjects, has no right to impose a new tax. The consequence is that he permits the bashaws or governors of provinces to pillage the people without mercy; and, in turn, squeezes out of them the sums of which he stands in need, to satisfy his own exigencies and those of the state. In America, from a like cause, the government of the Union has gradually dwindled into a state of decay, approaching nearly to annihilation. Who can doubt, that the happiness of the people in both countries would be promoted by competent authorities in the proper hands, to provide the revenues which the necessities of the public might require?

The present Confederation, feeble as it is intended to repose in the United States, an unlimited power of providing for the pecuniary wants of the Union. But proceeding upon an erroneous principle, it has been done in such a manner as entirely to have frustrated the intention. Congress, by the articles which compose that compact (as has already been stated), are authorized to ascertain and call for any sums of money necessary, in their judgment, to the service of the United States; and their requisitions, if conformable to the rule of apportionment, are in every constitutional sense obligatory upon the States. These have no right to question the propriety of the demand; no discretion beyond that of devising the ways and means of furnishing the sums demanded. But though this be strictly and truly the case; though the assumption of such a right would be an infringement of the articles of Union; though it may seldom or never have been avowedly claimed, yet in practice it has been constantly exercised, and would continue to be so, as long as the revenues of the Confederacy should remain dependent on the intermediate agency of its members. What the consequences of this system have been, is within the knowledge of every man the least conversant in our public affairs, and has been amply unfolded in different parts of these inquiries. It is this which has chiefly contributed to reduce us to a situation, which affords ample cause both of mortification to ourselves, and of triumph to our enemies.

What remedy can there be for this situation, but in a change of the system which has produced it in a change of the fallacious and delusive system of quotas and requisitions? What substitute can there be imagined for this ignis fatuus in finance, but that of permitting the national government to raise its own revenues by the ordinary methods of taxation authorized in every well-ordered constitution of civil government? Ingenious men may declaim with plausibility on any subject; but no human ingenuity can point out any other expedient to rescue us from the inconveniences and embarrassments naturally resulting from defective supplies of the public treasury.

passages.title: Thoreau — Deliberate Living and the Price of Progress
passages.text:
I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived. I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear; nor did I wish to practise resignation, unless it was quite necessary. I wanted to live deep and suck out all the marrow of life, to live so sturdily and Spartan-like as to put to rout all that was not life, to cut a broad swath and shave close, to drive life into a corner, and reduce it to its lowest terms, and, if it proved to be mean, why then to get the whole and genuine meanness of it, and publish its meanness to the world; or if it were sublime, to know it by experience, and be able to give a true account of it in my next excursion. For most men, it appears to me, are in a strange uncertainty about it, whether it is of the devil or of God, and have _somewhat hastily_ concluded that it is the chief end of man here to "glorify God and enjoy him forever."

Still we live meanly, like ants; though the fable tells us that we were long ago changed into men; like pygmies we fight with cranes; it is error upon error, and clout upon clout, and our best virtue has for its occasion a superfluous and evitable wretchedness. Our life is frittered away by detail. An honest man has hardly need to count more than his ten fingers, or in extreme cases he may add his ten toes, and lump the rest. Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity! I say, let your affairs be as two or three, and not a hundred or a thousand; instead of a million count half a dozen, and keep your accounts on your thumb-nail. In the midst of this chopping sea of civilized life, such are the clouds and storms and quicksands and thousand-and-one items to be allowed for, that a man has to live, if he would not founder and go to the bottom and not make his port at all, by dead reckoning, and he must be a great calculator indeed who succeeds. Simplify, simplify. Instead of three meals a day, if it be necessary eat but one; instead of a hundred dishes, five; and reduce other things in proportion. Our life is like a German Confederacy, made up of petty states, with its boundary forever fluctuating, so that even a German cannot tell you how it is bounded at any moment. The nation itself, with all its so-called internal improvements, which, by the way are all external and superficial, is just such an unwieldy and overgrown establishment, cluttered with furniture and tripped up by its own traps, ruined by luxury and heedless expense, by want of calculation and a worthy aim, as the million households in the land; and the only cure for it, as for them, is in a rigid economy, a stern and more than Spartan simplicity of life and elevation of purpose. It lives too fast. Men think that it is essential that the _Nation_ have commerce, and export ice, and talk through a telegraph, and ride thirty miles an hour, without a doubt, whether _they_ do or not; but whether we should live like baboons or like men, is a little uncertain. If we do not get out sleepers, and forge rails, and devote days and nights to the work, but go to tinkering upon our _lives_ to improve _them_, who will build railroads? And if railroads are not built, how shall we get to heaven in season? But if we stay at home and mind our business, who will want railroads? We do not ride on the railroad; it rides upon us. Did you ever think what those sleepers are that underlie the railroad? Each one is a man, an Irishman, or a Yankee man. The rails are laid on them, and they are covered with sand, and the cars run smoothly over them. They are sound sleepers, I assure you. And every few years a new lot is laid down and run over; so that, if some have the pleasure of riding on a rail, others have the misfortune to be ridden upon. And when they run over a man that is walking in his sleep, a supernumerary sleeper in the wrong position, and wake him up, they suddenly stop the cars, and make a hue and cry about it, as if this were an exception. I am glad to know that it takes a gang of men for every five miles to keep the sleepers down and level in their beds as it is, for this is a sign that they may sometime get up again.
